thesis: Ending a session preserves freedom when further possibility no longer adds relevant value.

ideas.statement: Separate exploration, execution, evaluation and rest; stop for success, no progress, missing evidence or fatigue.
The casino analogy itself requires experiments that compare persistence with verified gains.

evidenceAndExamples.statement: At some point, a conversation must end. Not because everything that could be said has been exhausted, but because life cannot be organized around exhausting possibility.

An LLM can always offer another perspective. This abundance is one of its powers. Without a stopping criterion, it can also become a way of postponing contact with the concrete thing: the program put to the test, the chapter offered to a reader, the hypothesis confronted with data, the conversation with the person we have discussed for hours.

We propose four modes of work that should not be continually mixed. In exploration, we seek possibilities and accept provisionality. In execution, we choose a direction and build. In evaluation, we try to determine whether the result deserves acceptance. In rest, we have no obligation to prepare the next optimization.

Moving between modes must be possible. An experiment can reopen exploration. A new problem can require redefining the task. But if every evaluation becomes a new list of ideas, no result ever meets a verdict.

A useful ritual is to write at the outset what kind of session we want. “Tonight I am exploring metaphors” allows joy without a claim to proof. “I am checking a claim” requires evidence and tolerance for disappointment. Confusion arises not from the existence of both activities but from switching them without notice.

We can stop because we met the criterion. We can stop because there is no further relevant progress. We can stop because we identified necessary external evidence. We can stop because we are tired and no longer evaluating well. None of the latter reasons is shameful.

A practical question is: what would the next attempt need to bring to justify its cost? We need not calculate an exact formula. Distinguishing possible new information from merely repeating the same hope is enough.

If ten versions have the same fundamental error, perhaps we need to change the method rather than ask for an eleventh. If the necessary source is unavailable, more elegant wording will not produce it. If the problem requires a discussion with a beneficiary, another plan does not replace that discussion.

In some situations, we seek the best answer we can obtain. In others, we seek one good enough for the purpose at a reasonable cost. A chapter title can have a thousand successful variants. Choosing one does not declare all the others inferior for eternity.

A generative tool makes the abundance of alternatives visible. This does not create an obligation to examine them all. Freedom to choose includes the freedom not to buy, with our time, the impossible certainty that we never missed a better version.

For serious decisions, the evidence threshold must be higher. But ritual checking without new information does not help there either. A relevant second opinion, a test, or an independent source can matter more than a hundred reformulations of the same reassurance.

The casino metaphor must itself be verified. We can design nonclinical studies varying the irregularity of output quality while preserving, as far as possible, the same average quality and costs. We observe whether participants continue longer and actually obtain greater value. Task difficulty, experience, latency, and the type of feedback should be controlled.

A second experiment would compare real control with apparent control: do users’ changes actually alter the chance of success or merely the presentation? A third would test whether a progress record and a stopping criterion reduce unproductive repetition without suppressing useful discoveries.

For coding agents, we can compare the number of tasks launched with the number independently accepted, review time, subsequent errors, and reported workload. What matters is not treating satisfaction as the only criterion, but not ignoring it either. An activity can become simultaneously more efficient and more enjoyable; that would be a success, not a cause for suspicion.

These proposals were not carried out for the book. They are a program for testing its ideas. If results showed that variety increases both continuation and verified value, we would have reasons to defend certain forms of it. If only duration increases, we would face a different problem. A useful metaphor must be able to lose to the data.

We need not become permanent auditors. We can use AI for play, poetry, learning, and exploration without demanding a solemn accounting from every conversation. What must be protected is our ability to recognize which activity we are engaged in and change activities when it no longer serves us.

The book began with a boundary between control and chance. It reaches another boundary: between possibility that expands our freedom and possibility that occupies all our time. Neither can be established by technology alone. We need criteria, institutions, relationships, and personal choices.

We can ask a great deal of these tools. We can ask for explanations, ideas, programs, and even contributions to real discoveries. But we need not also delegate to them the definition of the moment when we have lived enough for today.

objectionsAndQualifications.statement: Proposed studies not performed; useful variety and unaccounted play remain legitimate.

audit.notes: Complete chapter read; preserve proposed concepts, empirical limits and non-diagnostic distinctions.
